title: Charts that mislead
objectives: Spot truncated axes and cherry-picked windows, and fix them
Choose the figure shape and annotations so a chart tells the truth

screens.title: Pick a year, any year
screens.prose: A fund's unit price over 36 months. Its factsheet may show any 12 months it likes. Slide the shaded window to choose the start month and watch its return.
screens.question: What is the best 12-month return you can find, in %?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start the window at the bottom of the fall and read the caption.

byKey.first: That is the first window, months 0 to 12. Slide on and look for the best one.

explain.text: Starting at the low in month 14 gives +42.5%, the window a factsheet would love. Starting at month 0 gives −23.2%. Same fund, same prices: only the window changed.

screens.title: The whole history
screens.prose: Choosing the window that flatters is **cherry-picking** a window. Here is the fund's full history, with the factsheet's window shaded. It started at £100.00 and ended at £97.76.
screens.question: What did the fund return over all 36 months, in %?

hints.text: Divide the last price by the first.
The first is £100.00 and the last £97.76.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the first and last prices of the whole history.

byKey.pick: That is the factsheet's window again. Use month 0 and month 35.

explain.text: Over all 36 months the fund lost 2.24%. The factsheet's +42.5% is true, but it starts at the bottom of a 26% fall. Show the whole period, or say why the window starts where it does.

screens.title: Tall or wide
screens.prose: Both panels plot the same 30 daily closes, a rise of 4%, on the same y range of £99 to £105. Only the figure's shape differs: `figsize=(4, 6)` on top, `figsize=(8, 3)` below.
screens.question: A colleague shows the top panel as proof of a surge. What made it look steeper?

options.text: Only the shape of the figure: taller and narrower
A truncated y axis
options.why: Both panels run from £99 to £105. The axis is the same; the box is not.

options.text: More days of data
options.why: Both panels hold the same 30 closes.

options.text: A log scale on the top panel
options.why: Both axes are ordinary. A log scale would make the rise look slightly smaller, not steeper.

hints.text: Compare the two panels' y ranges and data first.
Both hold the same closes on the same range.
The top box is tall and narrow, so the same rise climbs more steeply.

feedback.correct: Same data, same axis, different box.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. List what is the same in the two panels, then what differs.

explain.text: Slope on the page is height over width, so a tall box steepens every move. Keep one shape, such as `figsize=(8, 4.5)`, for every time series you compare.

screens.title: An annotation that explains
screens.prose: You are annotating the strategy's 60-day equity curve for a client note. An annotation should tell the reader something they would otherwise have to work out.
screens.question: Which annotation explains rather than decorates?

options.text: “Max drawdown −9.9%: day 18 to day 33”
“Ouch”
options.why: It points at the fall but tells the reader nothing they cannot see.

options.text: An arrow pointing at day 33, with no text
options.why: An arrow says “look here” but not what to see.

options.text: “Peak” and “Trough” in large red letters
options.why: It names points the reader can already see, and red adds alarm without a number.

hints.text: Which one adds a fact the reader could not read off the chart at a glance?
Only one gives a number and a period.
The drawdown annotation states the size and the dates of the fall.

feedback.correct: A number and a period: the reader learns something.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for the annotation that carries a fact.

explain.text: The good annotation gives the size of the fall and when it happened, facts the reader would otherwise measure. In matplotlib, `ax.annotate(text, xy=(33, 9671.68))` puts it beside the trough.

screens.title: Two bar charts, one fall
screens.prose: A stock closed at £98.00 on Monday and £96.04 on Friday, a fall of 2%. Both charts draw these two closes as bars.
screens.question: Which chart misleads?

options.text: Chart A
Chart B
options.why: Chart B looks flat because the fall is small: £1.96 on £98.00. Its bars start at zero, so their lengths are honest.

options.text: Neither: both label the same two closes correctly
options.why: The tick labels are right on both, but readers judge a bar by its length. On Chart A, Friday's bar is a third of Monday's.

hints.text: A bar shows its value by its length. Where does each chart's bar start?
Chart A's bars start at £95.00, not at zero.
On Chart A, Friday's bar is about a third of Monday's, for a 2% fall.

feedback.correct: Chart A cuts the bars off at £95.00.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the bar lengths with the real 2% fall.

byKey.neither: You checked the numbers, which are right on both. But a bar is read by its length, and Chart A starts at £95.00. Its Friday bar is a third of Monday's, for a 2% fall.
byKey.b: You picked the chart where the fall looks small. It is small: 2%. Chart B's bars start at zero, so it tells the truth.

explain.text: Chart A starts its axis at £95.00, so it shows only the tops of the bars, and a 2% dip reads as a collapse. Bars must start at zero. Chart B looks dull because the move was dull.

screens.title: How big the fall looks
screens.prose: On Chart A the drawn part of Monday's bar runs from £95.00 to £98.00, and Friday's from £95.00 to £96.04. The eye compares those two lengths.
screens.question: What fall does Chart A appear to show?

options.why: That is the true fall, which Chart B shows. Chart A's eye-reading uses the drawn lengths.

options.text: About −35%
options.why: That is $1.04 / 3.00$ itself, the share left. The fall is that share minus 1.

options.text: About −1.96%
options.why: That is the £1.96 drop read as a percentage of £100. The drawn lengths are 3.00 and 1.04.

hints.text: Compare the drawn lengths as if they were the values.
Monday's drawn length is 3.00 and Friday's is 1.04.

feedback.correct: A 2% fall drawn to look like 65%.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work from the drawn lengths, 3.00 and 1.04.

explain.text: Chart A draws lengths of 3.00 and 1.04, so the eye sees $1.04 / 3.00 - 1 = -65\%$. The true fall is 2%: the chart exaggerates it more than thirtyfold. On Chart B the lengths are the values themselves.

screens.title: An honest chart, in code
screens.prose:
The checks you made, as code:

```python
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5))  # one shape for every chart you compare
ax.bar(days, closes)
ax.set_ylim(0, max(closes) * 1.1)         # bars start at zero
ax.plot(dates, prices)                    # a line may zoom to its range
# show the whole period, or say why the window starts there
# annotate with a number, not a mood
```
screens.question: A line chart of daily closes between £96 and £99. Must its y axis start at zero?

options.text: No: a line is read by its position, so a tight range is fine if labelled
Yes: every chart must start at zero
options.why: Bars are read by length, so they need zero. A line is read by position; from zero, a £3 range would be a flat line.

options.text: No, but it must use a log axis
options.why: Over £96 to £99 a log axis looks almost the same as an ordinary one.

feedback.correct: Zero is a rule for bars, not lines.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask how the reader reads each kind of mark.

explain.text: A bar's length is its value, so cutting the bar lies. A line's height is read against labelled ticks, so zooming in is honest. The zoom only misleads if the ticks are hidden.

screens.title: Fix the chart
screens.prose: A morning note went out with Chart A. Fix `fixed_bars` so the bars start at zero, and print each close on its bar as `£98.00`. `ax.bar_label(bars, fmt="£%.2f")` or `ax.text` will do it.
screens.question: Complete `fixed_bars(days, closes)`.

widget.solution:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")  # draw to files, not a window
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def fixed_bars(days, closes):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
    bars = ax.bar(days, closes)
    ax.set_ylim(0, max(closes) * 1.1)
    ax.bar_label(bars, fmt="£%.2f")
    ax.set_ylabel("Close (£)")
    return fig, ax
widget.how: Check runs 3 hidden tests on the figure your function returns. The first run loads matplotlib, a large package, so it can take up to 20 seconds; later runs are quick.

hints.text: Start the axis at 0, with room above the taller bar.

feedback.correct: Honest bars, with the exact closes printed for anyone who needs them.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the failing test: it names what it checked.

explain.text: From zero the two bars look nearly equal, which is the truth. The printed values keep the exact move readable: £98.00 to £96.04. Deleting `set_ylim` also works, since matplotlib starts bars at zero by itself.

ideas: Bars are read by length, so a bar chart's axis starts at zero. A line may zoom to its range when its ticks are labelled.
The window is a choice: show the whole history, or say why it starts where it does.
Keep one figure shape for charts you compare, and annotate with numbers, not moods.

formula.name: The fall a truncated bar chart suggests
formula.note: With the axis starting at $b$. Only $b = 0$ gives the true change $p_1 / p_0 - 1$.

summary.trap: Correct tick labels do not make a bar chart honest: readers judge bars by length, and a truncated axis cuts the lengths.

quiz.prose: A bar chart's y axis starts at £50. One bar is £60.00 and the next is £57.00, a fall of 5%.
quiz.question: What fall do the drawn bar lengths suggest, in %?

feedback.correct: Lengths of 10 and 7 look like a 30% fall.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Measure each bar from £50, not from zero.

byKey.true: That is the true fall. The drawn bars start at £50, so they are 10 and 7 long.
byKey.share: That is the share left, 7 / 10. The fall is that minus 1.

explain.text: From £50 the bars are 10 and 7 long, so the eye reads $7/10 - 1 = -30\%$. The true fall is 5%, six times smaller.

quiz.prose: A fund's factsheet charts its performance “since 23 March 2020”, the day markets hit their low in the pandemic sell-off.
quiz.question: What is the problem with that chart?

options.text: The start date is the bottom of a fall, so any recovery looks like skill
Four years is too short for any chart
options.why: Four years can be fine. The problem is where the window starts.

options.text: It should use a log axis
options.why: An axis choice cannot repair a flattering start date.

options.text: Nothing, if the numbers are correct
options.why: Correct numbers over a cherry-picked window still mislead.

feedback.correct: Starting at the low flatters every fund.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask why that date was chosen.

explain.text: Almost every fund rose from that low, so the chart shows the market's rebound as the fund's gain. An honest chart shows a standard period, such as five years, or the whole history.

quiz.prose: Three charts for a daily risk report.
quiz.question: Which one must start its y axis at zero?

options.text: Bars of each desk's P&L in £
A line of the FTSE 100 level over a week
options.why: A line is read by position against labelled ticks, so a tight range is honest.

options.text: A scatter of two stocks' daily returns
options.why: A scatter is read by position too. Zero is in the middle of most return scatters anyway.

options.text: A log chart of an index over 30 years
options.why: A log axis has no zero at all.

feedback.correct: Bars are read by length, so they need zero.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the mark read by its length.

explain.text: Only bars encode a value as a length, and a length only means something from zero. Lines and dots are read by position, so they may zoom.

quiz.prose: A chart of a strategy's equity needs one annotation at its worst fall.
quiz.question: Which line of matplotlib adds the most useful one?

options.text: `ax.annotate("−12.4% in 18 days", xy=(41, 8760))`
`ax.annotate("Look here", xy=(41, 8760))`
options.why: It points but tells the reader nothing new.

options.text: `ax.set_title("A bad patch")`
options.why: A title is not an annotation, and “bad” is a mood, not a fact.

options.text: `ax.axvspan(23, 41, color="red")`
options.why: A red band marks the dates but gives no size, and red alone fails colour-blind readers.

feedback.correct: Size and length of the fall, at the spot.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Prefer the annotation that carries numbers.

explain.text: An annotation earns its place by stating a fact the reader would otherwise measure: here, how deep and how long the fall was.
